subject: hedgehog
pitch: A plump hedgehog out on an autumn evening walk. A dome of spines in chestnut brown with cream tips, a soft fawn face with a pointed, twitchy snout, a shiny black button nose, tiny round ears and bright beady eyes. Little pink paws, and a single red maple leaf stuck on its spines like a trophy.
reasoning:
I'm planning out a hedgehog model as a single TypeScript module using the SDK, sketching proportions for the body dome and figuring out how to scatter spine geometry (cones or sticks) across the surface for a realistic look.

For the spines, I realize using a paint function on each spike sweep lets me color chestnut at the base and cream near the tip based on the parameter t, which is cleaner than trying to stick separate tip pieces onto each spine and keeps the part count well under the 1000 limit with ~150 spikes.

Now I'm sketching out the body structure: a spine chain running from rear to front using a catmull curve, then building the main body as a sweep with varying radius stations to shape the hedgehog's rounded silhouette, while being careful to only import the builder functions I actually need to avoid unused-import errors.

For the head, I'll angle it forward and slightly down, giving it a fawn-colored sphere with a tapered snout cone for the face. I'm setting up a spine chain with multiple joints to carry the body curve into the head attachment point.

Still naming the joints...

Legs will be short hidden capsules mostly tucked under the body, with little pink paw spheres scaled into ellipsoid shapes peeking out at the base. Ears will be tiny spheres half-sunk into the sides of the head, positioned using local head coordinates.

Still working out the sign conventions...

Now I'm planning the facial features: beady black eye spheres positioned on the sides of the head, a black button nose at the snout tip, and the head shape itself built as a tapered sweep from a wider skull to a narrower pointed snout, using bezier path points in model space anchored at the neck joint.

I also need to rethink the spine chain's joint placement — with a catmull path across multiple spans, joints sit at span starts rather than exactly where I want "back" and "neck" to be, so I'm reworking the chain to use three named joints (hips, chest, neck) across enough spans to position them correctly.

Actually, maybe the chain isn't essential for rigging at all here — simpler to just sweep the body geometry and skip strict joint correspondence, while still defining a clean spine path from the lower back through the chest up toward the head.

For the body radius, I'm shaping it as a smooth sine curve going from roughly 0.07 at the rump up to a peak near 0.088–0.09 at the midsection, then tapering again, checking carefully that the belly doesn't sink below the ground plane by validating it against the path's y-values at each sampled t.

Now I'm thinking through how the spines get scattered across the body surface — generating a few hundred candidates, filtering out the belly and the face/head region so they only sit on top and sides, then placing each one as a small spike mesh oriented along the surface normal with its own length and radius.

I'm tilting each spike's direction slightly backward along z so the spines sweep back naturally like a real hedgehog, then adding a cream-tipped color variation based on position along the spike's length.

For coloring, I'll use simple bands instead of a custom paint function — chestnut at the base transitioning to cream near the tip, which is more reliable for the sweep geometry. For the body underneath the spines, I'm applying a countershading effect with dark chestnut on the back (mostly hidden) and fawn on the belly, plus a fawn-toned head and a small black sphere for the nose tip.

Now I'm figuring out the nose placement relative to where the pointed snout ends, since the "point" cap style extends the tip slightly beyond the geometry's defined end — so I'm nudging the nose sphere position to sit right at that extended point for a seamless look. For the ears, I'm planning to use a flattened cylinder disc oriented to face sideways rather than a sphere, to get a more natural ear shape.

Working out the ear placement next — positioning them near the top-back of the head using the neck joint's local coordinate frame, accounting for the spine's forward-up slope so they sit naturally among the spines rather than floating oddly.

I'm adding a small white highlight sphere to each eye for a glint effect, then positioning the pink paw spheres peeking out from under the body at the front and back.

Working out the scale and vertical positioning so the paws' bottoms just touch the floor without floating or clipping, adjusting the y-offset and flattening ratio to get it precise.

Now I'm shifting to designing the leaf stuck in the spines — planning a simplified maple leaf outline with five lobes, generating the outline points procedurally in a flat plane before extruding it into a thin 3D shape.

Generating leaf outline points...

I'll keep smoothing at 1 to soften edges while preserving the sharp tips of the lobes. For placement, I'm thinking of the leaf stuck on top of the body near the spines, like a trophy — positioning it on the back surface using a point found around the body sweep.

I'm working out the extrude orientation so the leaf outline sits in the horizontal plane with its thickness pointing vertically, letting it lie flat on top of the spines as if hovering just above or resting on their tips, poking through slightly to sell the "stuck" look.

I'm recalculating the actual body-top height since spines plus body radius push the total higher than expected, which changes where the leaf should rest and how the connecting pins or rods should be positioned underneath it to look pinned onto the spines.

Placing the outline tips at 0.05 radius centered at the leaf origin, with an unnormalized rotation basis for the extrude orientation. For color, I'm keeping the leaf red but considering a subtle darker vein running along the stem axis by painting based on the distance from the centerline.

Now I'm fleshing out the rest of the creature's palette: chestnut and cream for spine coloring, fawn for the face, black for nose and eyes, pink for paws, and a slightly darker fawn-pink for the ears. For the spines themselves, I'm working out the scatter parameters—around 260 spines with a base radius and length, filtered to avoid the belly and head regions using the hit normal's y-component and position checks.

I'm defining the spike direction using the surface normal with a backward tilt, and setting up a seeded random generator to vary each spine's length slightly. For coloring, I'm using a countershade gradient for the body and banded colors along each spike's length. But I'm realizing each spike with banding creates two parts, so 260 spines would generate roughly 520 parts total—I need to keep this under the 1000-part budget.

I'm estimating around 540 parts total is fine given triangle counts for 8-sided spikes with rings. Now I'm sketching the builder structure: creating the hedgehog with a root joint at the origin, then a spine chain under it, and sweeping the body geometry along that spine path using the countershade coloring and rounded caps.

Deciding whether to sweep over the spine chain directly so the skin follows the chain's roll smoothly, then shaping the head as a tapered cone from neck to snout with a pointed end cap and a quadratic-ish radius falloff for a more bulged skull narrowing to the nose.

I'm now checking the actual world-space positions along the head bezier curve to make sure the ears and eyes land correctly on the surface — computing midpoint and t=0.6 points, their radii, and placing eye spheres just outside the head radius at those coordinates. I'm concluding the head doesn't need spines since it's just fur-covered like a real hedgehog's face, while the body keeps the spiny texture.

Now I'm working out the nose placement right at the tip of the head curve, then positioning the ears near the back of the head using another bezier interpolation at t=0.3, sizing them as thin discs offset to the sides. Finally I'm calculating where the front and back paws should attach, checking the body's radius at those z-positions to make sure the paw spheres sit properly against the body surface rather than floating or clipping through it.

Pink paws should peek out at the belly edges, positioned symmetrically. I'm skipping toe details to save on budget and instead focusing on getting the spine scatter working correctly on the body surface, filtering out points near the head and tail so spines don't overlap those areas. I'm estimating triangle counts for the spike geometry and realizing the default sides count will push the total far too high, so I need to reduce the spike sides or lower detail to stay within budget.

Reducing spike sides to 5 and dropping the scatter count to around 240 should keep triangle totals manageable, while the body sweep itself can stay at default resolution since it only needs a couple rings. I'm planning a leaf resting on top of the spine tips rather than adding a separate stem, positioning it slightly tilted above the body's highest point, and attaching it to the nearest joint in the spine chain. Finally I'm adding a tiny white glint sphere near the eye for a bit of shine.

Working through eye placement now: computing the eye center's distance from the head's central axis to confirm it sits just outside the head sphere's surface, then calculating a glint offset that floats a touch further out along the same direction so it reads as a highlight rather than being swallowed into the eyeball.

Skipping the mouth for now and moving into the actual build code, I'm setting up the hedgehog's color palette, defining the builder with a root joint and a spine chain running from hips through chest to neck, with named segments for later bone attachment.

Still writing body geometry...

Verifying the spine's radius profile and vertical positions line up so the body's belly sits flush with the paws, then setting up a seeded random generator to scatter spine quills across the back surface, filtering out points that are too low or too far forward so they only appear on the upper back.

For each scattered point I'm spawning a small spike angled slightly backward, tapering from chestnut at the base to cream at the tip, to simulate fur/spine texture. Now I'm starting to build a star-shaped leaf outline using alternating outer and inner radius points around a circle...

Still writing leaf outline...

I'm placing the stem attachment at the bottom valley point of the outline, and applying smoothing so the sharp tips stay crisp while the valleys get gently rounded. Now I'm extruding that outline into a thin leaf shape, adding a bevel, and painting it so a thin central strip becomes a vein color while the rest stays leaf green, attaching it to a joint on the spine.

Now I'm double-checking the types line up for the paint callback and the tilt vector, then moving to write the head's bezier curve, add the meta export with name and description, and start a loop to build the paws symmetrically on both sides.

For the paws I'm scaling the sphere geometry directly rather than risking an unsupported scale option, applying it safely via BufferGeometry's own scale method for the body, ears, eyes, and nose — each sized and flattened slightly differently to read correctly as hedgehog features.

Writing geometry code...

Now I'm checking the proportions: the body's forward cap extends too far and would overlap the head, so I need to shorten the spine path so the body ends sooner and leaves room for the muzzle to sit in front without being buried.

Tuning the radius falloff function...

Now I'm tracing the head's bezier curve to find where eyes, nose, and ears should sit along the surface, computing approximate y/z coordinates and radii at several t-values so the facial features land naturally on the tapering head shape.

Checking the paws against the body's silhouette, I realize the front and back paw positions might sit slightly detached from the torso at belly height, so I'm nudging their x/y offsets inward so they visually overlap the body rather than floating beside it as disconnected shapes.

With the spine tips, leaf placement, and body colors (dark chestnut top fading to fawn belly) now settled, I'm starting to write out the full build script -- defining the root joint, a spine chain through hips/chest/neck via a Catmull-Rom curve, and continuing to assemble the skeleton from there.

Still adding body parts...
